preprints.title: A Unified Comparison of 10X Genomics and Parse Biosciences scRNA-seq Technologies
preprints.abstract: Droplet-based and split-pool barcoding are the two dominant high-throughput single-cell RNA-seq paradigms, yet their systematic biases remain incompletely characterized. We compared seven matched 10X Genomics Chromium and Parse Biosciences Evercode WT sample pairs from five studies spanning multiple tissues and species focusing on gene counts and compositional differences rather than cell-type resolution. By separating Parse reads by priming strategy, we distinguished biases arising from priming chemistry from platform-level effects. These effects were largely independent, with platform-level differences substantially larger. Priming strategy introduced a GC-content bias within Parse, whereas the two platforms showed a consistent compositional shift across priming strategies, supported by differential capture of nuclear- and cytoplasmic-enriched transcripts. We interpret this shift as a relative enrichment of nuclear RNA in Parse. Finally, using contamination measures that do not assume a droplet-specific model, we found background RNA contamination in Parse to be comparable in magnitude to that in 10X, contrary to claims of substantially lower contamination. Together, these results indicate that expression measurements and cell-type composition are not directly interchangeable between the two platforms.

last_author.name: Hallgrimsdottir, I. B.
last_author.affiliation: California Institute of Technology

preprints.title: A tissue-targeted auxin-inducible degradation toolkit for C. elegans embryogenesis
preprints.abstract: Many proteins required for embryogenesis are expressed in multiple tissues and across developmental time, often with tissue- and stage-specific roles. To resolve where and when proteins function, we developed a tissue-targeted auxin-inducible degradation toolkit for C. elegans embryogenesis. We generated a plasmid set compatible with single-copy insertion or high-copy extrachromosomal array generation that employs tissue-specific promoters (active in the germline, intestine, muscle, pharynx, neuroblasts, neurons, sensory neurons, epidermis, and pan soma) to drive an operon expressing an optimized auxin-dependent plant F-box factor TIR1 and, in most cases, a fluorescent histone. Using a ubiquitous nuclear envelope marker as a test substrate, we identified single-copy insertions and arrays that exhibit efficient auxin-dependent, tissue-specific target degradation. We also establish a workflow that ensures all functionally important isoforms of a target are tagged and that degradation reproduces the loss-of-function phenotype prior to tissue-specific analysis. Applying the toolkit to the broadly expressed Rho kinase LET-502, we find that degradation in the epidermis, but not in other embryonic tissues, disrupts elongation. Unexpectedly, temporal analysis revealed that LET-502 is required for late as well as early elongation.

last_author.name: Oegema, K.
last_author.affiliation: University of California San Diego

preprints.title: A unified framework for quantitative splicing and transcript prediction
preprints.abstract: RNA splicing is frequently disrupted by genetic variation, contributing to a wide range of human diseases. Identifying the variants responsible for altered splicing is therefore crucial but has long been challenging. Deep learning models that predict splicing from genomic sequence have substantially advanced their detection, but accurately resolving their quantitative effects on splicing and the resulting transcripts remains an unmet need. Here we introduce SpliceAI2, a deep learning model trained end-to-end on splice site, splice junction, and transcript usage across multiple mammalian species. SpliceAI2 reconstructs complete transcripts directly from genomic sequence and considerably improves identification of splice-altering variants and quantification of their effects in diverse benchmarks spanning cryptic splicing, splicing quantitative trait loci, and massively parallel reporter assays. Human population datasets provide independent validation of these predicted functional effects through evidence of natural selection and associated changes in plasma protein abundance. Application to a rare disease cohort reveals that predicted splice-altering variants are highly enriched in disease-associated genes and account for 15% of the excess genetic burden, with approximately half residing in deep intronic regions likely missed by exome sequencing. Together, these findings establish SpliceAI2 as a major step forward in interpreting splice-altering variants across the human genome.

preprints.title: ALBIS: simulation of multi-resolution and multi-dimensional spatial transcriptomics data
preprints.abstract: The rapid adoption of spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies has been accompanied by substantial growth in computational methods, creating an increasing need for systematic and reliable benchmarking, particularly as analyses increasingly extend from individual tissue sections to three-dimensional (3D) tissue reconstruction. Existing benchmarks often rely on a small and similar set of experimentally-derived datasets because they offer a reliable ground truth label, which is hard to find in practice. Simulated or synthetic data provide an alternative, yet most existing simulators either adapt single-cell RNA-sequencing models to spatial coordinates or generate individual sections in a two-dimensional (2D) space at predefined resolutions. More recent approaches can simulate 2D and 3D tissues, but generally do not derive multiple spatial resolutions from the same molecular realization. Here, we introduce ALBIS (A muLti-resolution Biological In-silico Simulator for spatial transcriptomics), a statistically grounded and highly customizable framework that generates synthetic ST data from an in silico 3D tissue. ALBIS defines spatially structured cell populations with corresponding markers for gene expression, then initializes individual mRNA molecules in 3D space to create cell-level information with a ground truth 3D coordinate for each molecule and cell. From this common realization, ALBIS cuts the 3D tissue into multiple 2D tissue sections with cell-, bin-, and spot-level measurements, enabling direct comparison across spatial resolutions. Properties of the simulated data, including spatial domains, cell type composition, gene-expression effects, batch effects, measurement resolution, and tissue scale, can be systematically varied, enabling rigorous stress-testing of computational methods under known and increasingly challenging conditions.

preprints.title: Characterization of artificial riboswitches for Coxsackievirus B3 detection using machine learning
preprints.abstract: With the increase of recycled water to offset water demand, the potential possibility to spread contagious RNA viruses, such as Coxsackievirus B3, increases. However, detection of viral particles remains challenging because of low viral concentrations in wastewater and high mutation rates of the RNA virus. Robust monitoring is needed with low cost and low infrastructure technologies to increase accessibility of monitoring technologies worldwide. Novel viral detection methods have been developed, based on synthetic riboswitches that bind to the target virus and trigger a reporter gene, thus amplifying the detection signals. Such monitoring technologies can leverage machine learning to optimize the candidate nucleic acid sequences used for detection. To support the design of effective riboswitches, we present a machine learning model for classifying riboswitch performance, integrating RNA sequence data with secondary structural features based on free energy calculations and parameters that represent single strandedness. This model uses a sparsely gated Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture to route sequence and thermodynamic features to specialized experts, achieving strong generalization performance across cross-validation and held-out testing. When evaluated against baseline Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gaussian Naive Bayes, and Dense Neural Network classifiers, the MoE model demonstrated near-zero classification errors. Furthermore, post-hoc feature importance and k-mer analyzes reveal that near-perfect predictive performance in silico is strongly driven by sequence constructs in addition to generalizable folding mechanics. An ablation study of numerical feature and sequence inputs showed that while the Dense Neural Network also achieved high accuracy across all ablation conditions, the MoE architecture was retained as the primary model because its specialized subnetworks do not require all model parameters to be activated offering a potential computational advantage.

last_author.name: Andreopoulos, W. B.
last_author.affiliation: Department of Computer Science, San Jose State University

preprints.title: Fine-tuning genomic models on rare splicing events identifies a novel biomarker of TDP-43 pathology
preprints.abstract: Genomic foundation models (GFMs) are pretrained on large genomic datasets, but their ability to predict rare disease-associated events after fine-tuning remains unclear. We tested this using TDP-43 cryptic exons, well characterized splicing events linked to neurodegenerative disease that are poorly represented in standard annotations. We compared the state-of-the-art GFM AlphaGenome with OpenSpliceAI, a specialized splice site prediction model. Fine-tuned OpenSpliceAI detected held-out cryptic exons in human and mouse and captured allele-specific splicing effects at the disease-associated UNC13A locus. In contrast, a splicing prediction head trained on AlphaGenome's frozen pretrained backbone failed to predict cryptic exons. Unfreezing and fine-tuning all model weights, however, enabled AlphaGenome to generalize to held-out data. To investigate cryptic splicing in cell types that are difficult to study experimentally, we applied fine-tuned OpenSpliceAI across the genome to study cell type-specific genes. This led to the identification of new cryptic splicing events in CLDN11 and ARHGAP23, which were subsequently validated in FTLD-TDP brain tissue. Notably, the cryptic exon in CLDN11 is predicted to generate a neoepitope that could serve as an oligodendrocyte-specific biomarker of TDP-43 pathology. Our results show that even a state-of-the-art GFM can fail to generalize to rare splicing events, even with substantial pretraining. However, both foundation and specialized models that learn to generalize to rare biological events can have broad applications in biological discovery and medicine.

preprints.title: Geometric coordination of endothelial invasion and vascular patterning during epithelial morphogenesis
preprints.abstract: As organs grow and remodel in three dimensions, developing vascular networks extend through the tissue while maintaining spatial coordination and establishing connections between distant sprouts. How local endothelial behavior generates vascular patterns within such deforming environments remains poorly understood. Here, using the developing mouse epididymis, we combine two-photon live microscopy, pharmacological perturbations, and mathematical modeling to investigate angiogenesis alongside epithelial tubule folding. Endothelial cells invade the organ interior while maintaining proximity to the deforming tubule. Live imaging reveals dynamic protrusions directed toward the epithelium and a characteristic sequence in which endothelial fronts approach the tubule, stop, and maintain their separation despite continued folding. ERK activity promotes endothelial extension and declines during the transition to distance maintenance. From these observations, we derive a minimal follow-and-stop rule that captures endothelial positioning relative to the changing epithelium. Extending this model to three dimensions reveals how epithelial folding can bring otherwise distant endothelial fronts together, creating opportunities for vascular connection. Explants exhibiting greater three-dimensional folding also show a higher observed frequency of endothelial connections. Our findings support a geometric framework in which local endothelial dynamics and tissue-scale deformation can jointly contribute to vascular patterning during organ morphogenesis.

preprints.title: KDM6A Haploinsufficiency Is Insufficient to Disrupt Cochlear Structure and Auditory Function in Mouse Models of Kabuki Syndrome Type 2
preprints.abstract: Objective: Kabuki syndrome type 2 (KS2) is a rare X-linked disorder caused by pathogenic variants in KDM6A and is frequently associated with hearing impairment. Because auditory phenotypes include sensorineural, conductive, and mixed hearing loss, we examined whether Kdm6a deficiency directly impairs cochlear morphology or auditory function in mice. Methods: We generated Nestin-Cre; Kdm6a conditional mutants and a germline-derived global Kdm6a deletion model using Sox2-Cre-mediated germline recombination. Auditory function and cochlear morphology were assessed by auditory brainstem responses (ABRs), distortion product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAEs), and histological analyses. Results: Whole-body hemizygous or homozygous Kdm6a deletion resulted in embryonic lethality. Analyses therefore focused on Nestin-Cre; Kdm6aflox/Y males and females carrying a germline-derived heterozygous Kdm6a deletion. In Nestin-Cre mutants, ABR thresholds, wave I amplitudes and latencies, and DPOAE measures at 8, 16, and 32 kHz were comparable with littermate controls at 4 and 8 weeks. In heterozygous deletion females, ABR thresholds, wave I amplitudes and latencies at 4-64 kHz and DPOAE measures at 8, 16, and 32 kHz were comparable with male and female wild-type controls. No overt cochlear pathology was observed in either model. Conclusion: Kdm6a deficiency in the viable mouse models examined did not produce overt cochlear pathology or baseline auditory dysfunction. These findings suggest that partial Kdm6a loss alone is insufficient to produce a robust primary cochlear phenotype in young mice and highlight the potential contributions of non-cochlear, developmental, central, and later-onset mechanisms to hearing impairment in KS2. Clinically, these findings support careful evaluation for potentially treatable middle-ear disease.

last_author.name: Someya, S.
last_author.affiliation: University of Florida

preprints.title: Lack of adoption of computational gene-panel-selection tools in targeted spatial transcriptomics
preprints.abstract: Targeted spatial transcriptomics requires selecting a gene panel before any experiment is run. Choosing well across tens of thousands of candidate genes under platform-specific probe, panel-size, and sensitivity constraints is difficult to do manually, and impossible to correct once a panel has been used. A growing number of computational tools to automate this selection have been designed, yet it remains unclear whether they are adopted in practice. Several factors could limit uptake: validation uncertainty about panel performance, workflow friction between a ranked gene list and a submission-ready panel, limited platform awareness in tools developed for dissociated single-cell data, and the cost advantage of vendor panels. We analyzed 18 computational tools for gene-panel selection from two angles: their citation landscape and their use across a targeted spatial transcriptomics corpus. Across 540 full-text-classified records, only 35 (6.5%) reported using the cited tool for panel design; most came from computational, benchmark, review, or non-spatial papers, or papers that cited but did not use it. In an independent corpus, only 34 of 479 (7.1%) involved a computational tool, alone or in a hybrid workflow; most used manually curated, premade vendor, or modified vendor panels. Both lines of evidence point the same way: computational selection is rarely part of the reported experimental workflow, and it more often supplemented manual curation than replaced it. Adoption is unlikely to turn on further benchmark gains alone; it will depend on reducing the validation uncertainty and workflow friction that keep users on established panel-design practice.

last_author.name: Sifrim, A.
last_author.affiliation: Katholieke Universiteit Leuven

preprints.title: Perturb-Seqr: Signature Search Engine Integrating Connectivity Mapping Resources
preprints.abstract: High-throughput transcriptomics can be used to develop Connectivity Mapping resources for identifying potential reversers and mimickers of disease signatures for drug and target discovery. Recently, several new Connectivity Mapping datasets have emerged, but no efforts were made so far to evaluate and integrate them. Motivated by this opportunity, we have developed Perturb-Seqr, a comprehensive Connectivity Mapping search engine that integrates nine small molecule transcriptomics Connectivity Maps and seven single gene perturbation followed by expression Connectivity Maps. Specifically, Perturb-Seqr contains processed data from LINCS (L1000), Tahoe-100M, Novartis Institute for Biomedical Research (DRUG-seq), the original CMap (cDNA microarrays), Ginkgo Bioworks (DRUG-seq), SciPlex (scRNA-seq), DeepCover MoA (PISA proteomics), Perturb Atlas (RNA-seq), Replogle et al. (Perturb-seq), CREEDS (cDNA microarrays), CM4AI (Perturb-seq), and RummaGEO (RNA-seq). To serve these Connectivity Maps in one unifying search engine, we converted the expression signatures from these resources into 450,271 gene sets of up- and down-regulated genes measuring the effects of 9,856 unique drug and 17,643 unique gene perturbations, targeting 917 cell lines and cell types. We demonstrate how Perturb-Seqr, and the gene sets it serves, can be used to identify targets for drugs and drugs for targets, uncover new pathways, and identify potential side effects for preclinical compounds. Overall, Perturb-Seqr is a comprehensive up-to-date Connectivity Mapping search engine and database, enabling the discovery of new drugs and targets. Perturb-Seqr is accessible from: https://perturbseqr.maayanlab.cloud/.

preprints.title: Point-Process Modelling of Cell-Type Interaction Structure in CosMx Glioma Data for Hypothesis-Driven Tumor Inference from scRNA-seq
preprints.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) exhibits marked spatial heterogeneity that is lost after tissue dissociation for single-cell RNA sequencing. Here, we developed a spatial-statistical framework to characterize tumor-microenvironment organization and derive molecularly predictable spatial phenotypes from CosMx data. Eight GBM specimens comprising 2,427,362 cells, 15 cell populations, and four malignant states were analyzed, revealing substantial inter-patient differences in cellular composition and density. Fine finite-element meshes best preserved continuous spatial intensity and supported whole-tissue Log-Gaussian Cox Process modelling. Immune populations, including macrophages, microglia, monocytes, cDCs, neutrophils, and T cells, showed spatial attraction toward malignant states. These models generated cell-level measures of conditional intensity and tumor-proximity probability. Transcript abundances and metabolic pathway scores served as the sole predictive features to model these spatial phenotypes. Transcriptomic representations outperformed metabolic pathway scores. Leave-one-patient-out validation reduced predictive performance, and patient-wise harmonization failed to restore cross-patient transportability. Spatial outcome distributions varied between specimens, indicating that molecular-spatial relationships are strongly conditioned by patient-specific tumor architecture. Predicted interaction scores stratified transcriptional subclusters within cell types in external non-spatial single-cell datasets. This framework links spatial point-process phenotypes to molecular states and provides a basis for inferring spatial context from non-spatial single-cell data. Generalizing these models requires larger and more diverse spatial cohorts.
preprints.corresponding_institution: Ribeirão Preto Medical School - University of São Paulo

preprints.title: Towards Robust Automated Mouse Scratching Behavior Detection for Itch Research
preprints.abstract: Automated detection of mouse scratching behavior could reduce manual annotation and is essential for preclinical itch research. However, robust performance across laboratories remains a challenge for current methods. We present Scratch-AID+, a framework dedicated to automated mouse scratching detection, including a diverse and progressive set of approaches: classic ResNet-based detectors, task-adaptive fine-tuning of video foundation models, and in-context learning with advanced multimodal large language models. To simulate real-world use cases, we benchmark on a public dataset and utilize additional cross-laboratory video recordings for independent testing. We find that classic baselines suffered severe performance degradation on external data under the realistic setting with sparse scratching events. In contrast, fine-tuned video foundation models successfully bridged this generalizability gap, achieving significantly better detection performance. Furthermore, frozen multimodal large language models demonstrated promising out-of-the-box ability using only few-shot demonstrations. We also examined the effects of different video preprocessing strategies. Our findings highlight the improved performance and generalizability of the adapted foundation models for automated scratching behavior analysis and shed light on the real-world deployment of such detectors. Our code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/scratch aid-plus/.

preprints.title: cit_gsa: gene set analysis for scRNA-seq with covariate adjustment
preprints.abstract: Single-cell RNA-seq enables gene expression analysis at single-cell resolution. Differential Expression Analysis (DEA) performed at the gene set level for better power and interpretation, identifies gene sets associated with a factor of interest. Existing single-cell DEA methods rely on two-step approaches, a gene-level analysis followed by an enrichment step, are often limited to two-group comparisons and do not support covariate adjustment. We introduce cit_gsa, a novel one-step self-contained gene set DEA method for Single-cell RNA-seq that handles more than two conditions and allows covariate adjustment. A benchmark of cit_gsa against state-of-the-art methods shows that our method has better performance in complex scenarios, and real-data analysis confirms that covariate adjustment improves biological interpretation.
preprints.corresponding_institution: University of Bordeaux, Inserm Bordeaux Population Health, Inria SISTM, Vaccine Research Institute, Institut de Mathématiques de Toulouse

preprints.title: scGSCA: gene-set differential co-expression analysis for single-cell RNA sequencing data
preprints.abstract: Understanding disease-associated pathway coordination requires distinguishing phenotype-related co-expression changes from differences across cellular contexts while accounting for cells sampled from the same subject. Bulk gene-set co-expression methods do not directly address the sparse counts, single-cell distributional noise, subject-level dependence, and cell-type heterogeneity of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. We developed single-cell gene-set co-expression analysis (scGSCA), a framework for pathway-level differential co-expression analysis in scRNA-seq data. scGSCA fits gene-wise zero-inflated negative binomial mixed models with subject-level random effects and computes gene-set co-expression statistics from quantile residual correlations. It provides an overall differential gene-set co-expression analysis and an interaction test to assess whether the co-expression pattern between two cell types varies by sample phenotype. We applied scGSCA to tumor-normal gastric, breast-subtype, and lung-skin comparisons with matched bulk and scRNA-seq data. The overall test identified signals not captured in bulk analysis, including Axon guidance in gastric cancer and estrogen-response, IL6-JAK-STAT3, and TNF/NF-{kappa}B pathways in breast cancer. The interaction test further identified co-expression contrasts across cell types. scGSCA extends gene-set co-expression analysis to single-cell data while retaining subject-level structure and cell-type-specific context. scGSCA is freely available as an open-source R package.

last_author.name: Ye, F.
last_author.affiliation: University of Miami

preprints.title: 2,234 attempts to harmonize a multi-platform B-cell lymphoma bulk transcriptomic dataset: ComBat is superior by cross-batch prediction quality
preprints.abstract: Background. Cross-platform transcriptomic harmonization benchmarks rely on individual success metric each: correlation with a reference profile, classifier accuracy, or a composite imported from single-cell integration. We found no published study that computes multiple orthogonal metric classes over one set of harmonization approaches and measures overlapping between the best approaches by these metrics. Methods. We used the 2,234 approaches of the recent real-world benchmark on 7,174 B-cell lymphoma transcriptomes. They combine 31 harmonization methods, 14 batch-removal strategies, three imputations and two post-removal settings. We assigned its 87 polarity-adjusted scoring metrics, out of 344 registered, to five classes (global, local, distributional, structural and composite) and added three biology-facing classes: within-cohort marker correlation (L), cross-batch rank agreement of a marker panel (M), and leave-one-batch-out (LOBO) prediction of lymphoma subtypes and normal B cells (N). Each class resulted in top 112 approaches (5%), and we measured overlap by the Jaccard index. Results. Harmonization methods of high harshness such as quantile normalization matched different batches to the same shape of distribution but were inferior by local and global metrics. Local and composite metrics resulted in the largest overlap of best approaches (71 shared). Classes L and M, M and N shared no approach, whereas L and N shared one approach without harmonization under the rare-batches-removed strategy, and all three overlaps were significantly below the random expectation. Class N resulted in the ComBat family in 84 of its 112 places. Class M elected only 10_mnn and 12_scanorama, methods that completely corrupted biology by correlation. Conclusions. Best transcriptomic harmonization approach is highly contingent on the quality metrics used, with metric classes trade-offing between each other. We provide a six-step recipe for metric classes, their thresholds and the cross-batch tests for selecting the best approaches.
preprints.corresponding_institution: Institute of Molecular Biology, National Academy of Science of the Republic of Armenia, Yerevan, 0014, Armenia

preprints.title: A human-in-the-loop approach for faster cell tracking
preprints.abstract: Traditional cell tracking methods focus on fully automated tracking. The quality of the generated tracks, however, is heavily influenced by factors such as cell speed and density. In complex scenarios where track correctness is essential, an efficient and reliable tool for manual track correction remains a key component of the cell tracking process. Most tracking tools that allow for such manual correction do so only as a post-processing step, using human feedback to correct one track error at a time -- without improving the quality of other tracks in the dataset. This highlights the need for a more efficient track correction method that iteratively integrates human feedback into the automated tracking process. In this paper we propose a human-in-the-loop approach to cell tracking and investigate the extent to which a tracking algorithm can learn from human input during the tracking process. We combine a graph representation of cell detections, Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm, and a neural network that predicts cell displacement to generate initial track suggestions. We introduce a tool that enables human feedback on individual tracks suggested by the algorithm; this feedback is then propagated to improve subsequent track generation. Compared to the traditional approach of fully automated tracking with correction as a post-processing step, our human-in-the-loop tracking framework reduces the number of corrections required. Finally, we show how this approach can be integrated with existing state-of-the-art tracking algorithms by using pre-generated tracks as a prior, improving the quality of tracks suggested to the human annotator.

last_author.name: Textor, J.
last_author.affiliation: Radboudumc

preprints.title: A spatial topology atlas of type I myofibers in porcine skeletal muscle reveals local slow-oxidative niches associated with meat quality traits
preprints.abstract: Skeletal muscle metabolism and meat quality are usually interpreted through myofiber type composition, fiber size, and histochemical state. Whether the spatial topology of myofibers constitutes an independent phenotype layer remains poorly quantified. Here, using succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)-stained cross-sectional images from multiple pig breeds and more than 40 skeletal muscle sites, we established a multiscale spatial phenotyping framework for type I myofibers. To enable scalable instance-level quantification, we developed an improved Mask R-CNN segmentation workflow, trained with SAM-assisted and manually corrected annotations, and optimized for dense, small, irregular, and variably stained muscle fibers. This framework captures single-fiber morphology and staining, local contact, connected-cluster architecture, diffusion-ring neighborhoods, and global tissue configuration. Type I myofiber abundance was separable from spatial organization capacity: some muscles formed stronger-than-expected local connectivity and clustering despite modest type I fiber abundance. Spatial transcriptomic integration further showed that slow-oxidative genes and functional modules were non-randomly organized and formed local high-expression domains in type I fiber-enriched, high-contact neighborhoods. Across muscle sites and breeds, skeletal muscles displayed distinguishable type I fiber spatial topology identities, which were remodeled by breed background in a muscle-specific manner. In samples with matched meat-quality measurements, spatial topology features improved the explanation of pH, meat color, conductivity, and intramuscular fat. These results suggest that skeletal muscle should be modeled as a spatially organized tissue system rather than a simple mixture of fiber types.

last_author.name: Jin, L.
last_author.affiliation: Sichuan Agricultural University

preprints.title: A split-control criterion for few-shot adaptation in single-cell perturbation prediction
preprints.abstract: Few-shot adaptation can help or harm single-cell perturbation prediction, but conventional evaluation shares a control estimate between calibration responses and held-out targets. We show how methods carry control error into their predictions and derive its contribution to score inflation. Nested control-depth experiments support inverse-depth scaling of inner-product inflation; correlation inflation also depends on the control noise-to-signal ratio. Independent-control scoring changed the rank of 40 of 52 configuration-dataset entries. We introduce SafeDelta, a split-control criterion that uses calibration data to decide whether to adapt. Across six datasets, mean gated gain was non-negative under the original two-control evaluation. On a deep plate, fixed predictions and decisions retained positive mean gains under three additional independent control references. The same reproducibility principle identified a fibrosis programme that localises to scar in human liver. These results inform adaptation decisions and control-depth planning.

last_author.name: He, R.-R.
last_author.affiliation: Macau University of Science and Technology, Macau, China; Jinan University, Guangzhou, China; Institute for Intelligent Bioinnovation, Knowledge Transfer Center

preprints.title: A zebrafish ribosomopathy links Ddx49-dependent ribosome biogenesis to differential failure of population expansion among pigment cell lineages
preprints.abstract: Defects in ribosome biogenesis cause surprisingly cell-type specific pathologies. Why some cells are more vulnerable than others remains unresolved. Here, we show that a zebrafish pigment pattern mutant, sisley, results from a viable missense allele of ddx49, encoding a DEAD-box RNA helicase required for small ribosomal subunit biogenesis and early survival. In mutants, yellow/orange xanthophores fail to proliferate during development of the adult stripe pattern, whereas closely related melanophores are affected only mildly. The mutant protein has reduced helicase but increased ATPase activity and, consistent with impaired ribosome biogenesis in vivo, mutants are deficient in 18S rRNA relative to its precursor. Remarkably, a similar deficiency in 18S rRNA relative to precursor rRNA distinguishes xanthophores from melanophores even in the wild-type, suggesting an inherent difference in rRNA processing that leaves xanthophores vulnerable to Ddx49 dysfunction. Both xanthophore deficiency and a male-biased sex ratio of the sisley mutant were rescued by mutation of tp53. Our findings suggest how baseline differences in ribosome production shape cell-type specific outcomes of mutations affecting ribosome biogenesis, and provide an adult-viable model for Ddx49 function in vivo.

last_author.name: Parichy, D. M.
last_author.affiliation: University of Virginia

preprints.title: Ab initio CryoEM maps minimizing preferred orientation problems in heterogeneous mixtures: ReconSIREN
preprints.abstract: Cryo-Electron Microscopy (CryoEM) Single Particle Analysis (SPA) is pivotal for elucidating protein structures and their conformational dynamics. Several critical steps are required to obtain accurate maps. First, the \textit{ab initio} relative orientations and shifts between images must be determined. Second, the common issue of specimens presenting a preferred orientation should be adequately addressed. Third, all of the above must account for particle flexibility and sample heterogeneity. Additionally, these steps are interrelated, making the search for all these parameters a real challenge when considering convergence robustness. In this context, we present ReconSIREN, a novel deep learning framework that addresses the key steps outlined before in an \textit{ab initio} manner while greatly minimizing one of the most important practical burdens in SPA, namely the errors introduced in the CryoEM maps by the existence of preferred orientations; the latter is achieved by a change of the optimization approach that avoids the so-called ``attraction problem'', and by the introduction of a new type of geometrical priors. It does so fully \textit{ab initio}, using deep learning training/inference steps without resorting to more traditional optimization approaches, and generating highly accurate initial reconstructions. We present maps as both homogeneous (consensus) maps and a full conformational landscape for analyzing flexibility and heterogeneity. Thanks to its Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, ReconSIREN distributes the estimation workload across independent experts, improving optimization efficiency and simplifying the process.

preprints.title: Alpha Spatial: Language-guided prediction of single-cell spatial gene expression from histology
preprints.abstract: Routine histology preserves tissue architecture but leaves its molecular organization largely unmeasured. Recovering this information requires learning across heterogeneous gene panels and constraining a biologically ill-posed morphology-to-expression mapping. Here we present Alpha Spatial (AS), a language-conditioned framework that predicts cell-level gene expression from histology while jointly learning from different tissues and panels. Matched biological context improved prediction over omitted context, whereas incompatible context reduced accuracy. Multi-tissue learning further improved breast-tissue prediction, and AS outperformed the evaluated methods while preserving molecular-state organization. In breast cancer, AS recovered POSTN-associated stromal programmes and HER2-associated molecular and spatial differences. Exploratory patient-level analyses identified a CXCL14-associated spatial state whose abundance was associated with non-response to trastuzumab-containing treatment and larger residual invasive tumours. These findings establish a framework for reusing heterogeneous molecular observations to investigate tissue organization and treatment-associated microenvironments in archived histology.

preprints.title: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Frontier and Local LLMs Querying a Biomedical Knowledge Graph
preprints.abstract: We combine GeneNetwork's 1TB structured database with its metadata as an RDF graph and an associated literature corpus. We benchmark frontier and local LLMs querying it through four architectures: document, graph and agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a combination of the three. We evaluate them on 40 domain specific expert-curated questions with a new metric: the satisfaction frequency psi (psi, i.e, the share of questions answered with precision and recall of at least 70% or an f1 of at least 60%). psi ranks systems the same way precision, recall and f1 -- a machine learning metric built from the harmonic mean of precision and recall -- but is easier to read and assess for humans. System architecture had a large effect: with full use of Claude Opus 4.8 the plain document RAG of our earlier GNQA system had a psi of 36% against 86% for our new combined tools. Delegating most of the work from Claude Opus 4.8 to a local model halved query costs while still reaching a psi of 59%.

last_author.name: Prins, P.
last_author.affiliation: University of Tennessee Health Science Center

preprints.title: AnnZarro: scalable, interactive exploration of cell-by-cell and gene-by-gene relationships in single-cell data
preprints.abstract: Cell-by-cell and gene-by-gene relationships, such as kernels and correlations, shape most single-cell analyses but are rarely inspected directly due to a lack of visualization tools that display them. AnnZarro is a point-and-click browser viewer that shows these matrices linked to an AnnData object's cells x genes data. Using AnnZarro, experimental biologists can explore data without code and computational biologists can probe the relationships behind their analyses. One focused cell and one focused gene drive every panel. Clicking a cell paints its row of any cell-by-cell matrix over an embedding or spatial coordinates; clicking a gene paints its row of any gene-by-gene matrix over a gene plot such as a volcano. The focus also links genes to the cells where they change, and cells to the genes that distinguish them. AnnZarro reads only the matrix rows and columns each panel displays from zarr stores and hence users can explore matrices far larger than memory on a laptop or a shared server. Large datasets open on a reproducible subset, and users step through the remaining cells in parts. On a laptop, a 100,000-cell part of Tahoe-100M opens in 4 s and stays interactive. With the subset switched off, AnnZarro draws all 95.6 million cells in one plot in about 5 to 7 s. This tutorial prepares a dataset with Kompot differential abundance and expression, a diffusion kernel and gene correlations, then explores it in six worked examples.

last_author.name: Setty, M.
last_author.affiliation: Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center

preprints.title: Archetype analysis of multiplexed antibody imaging reveals interpretable morphological programs in optical pooled screens
preprints.abstract: High-content imaging-based screens with small molecule or genetic perturbations rely on rich optical phenotypes, yet how distinct subcellular markers contribute complementary biological information remains unclear. Here, we introduce CellMAPP, a multiplexed organelle imaging platform that uses optical pooled screens with iterative antibody staining to map cellular architecture under perturbation. Using 17 markers across 524 genetic perturbations in MCF-7 cells, we systematically examined how individual, and combinations of, markers capture diverse morphological responses. We find that markers provide complementary views of perturbation effects, with increased multiplexing improving signal and the breadth of hit recovery, although some phenotypes are better recovered from a subset of features rather than a full profile. Because non-molecular image-based profiles can be challenging to link with interpretable biology, we developed CHART (available at https://github.com/Genentech/CHART), an archetype analysis framework that identifies distinct reference morphological states for each marker and uses multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to automatically annotate them, connecting cellular images to recognizable organelle phenotypes. Integrating archetypes across multiple markers revealed modular morphological programs that describe coordinated organelle reorganization in response to perturbation. This framework identified regulators of defined organelle states such as micronuclei, nominated novel gene functions and revealed complex patterns of multi-organelle reposition. Together, optical profiling with MAPP and CHART provides an interpretable, scalable framework for image-based screens that sheds light on rules governing cellular structural reprogramming.

last_author.name: Regev, A.
last_author.affiliation: Genentech

preprints.title: Autonomous AI agents discover reverse transcriptases with tandem repeat arrays
preprints.abstract: Metagenomic databases hold vast quantities of unexplored genetic material that can seed tools for biotechnology and medicine, but discovery is limited by our ability to examine sequence data at scale. Here, we show that large language models (LLMs) in an autonomous harness can alleviate this bottleneck and surface novel molecular systems. We deployed Claude Code instances to survey reverse transcriptase (RT) loci across 1.9 billion protein clusters. Among the top candidates were array-associated RTs (ART), a novel family of jumbo-phage RTs coupled with an array of ~200-nucleotide units and a dedicated partner gene. Session transcripts show that Claude identified the ART family by directly examining its DNA sequences and recognizing the atypical repeats, a behavior attributable to specific Mythos 5 internal signals that respond to repeated DNA. ART arrays are highly expressed and appear as discrete units during Staphylococcus phage infection, suggesting an RT system directed by a repertoire of distinct RNAs. These findings indicate that LLMs can autonomously detect anomalies and drive analyses to initiate biological discoveries.

preprints.title: Beyond the gene: contextualizing novel isoforms through pathway analysis in long-read single-cell RNA sequencing
preprints.abstract: Differential isoform usage has been reportedly associated with distinct contexts associated with cell-type and disease; however, the mechanistic role that individual isoforms play in these contexts is poorly understood. Long-read single-cell RNA sequencing enables greater resolution into genes and isoforms previously difficult to detect via short-read approaches, including pseudogenes and those with repetitive motifs. This technique, combined with isoform-discovery tools such as Bambu, has yielded thousands of newly discovered isoforms and genes for consideration. The functional relevance of these new isoforms, however, remains enigmatic. Tools to prioritize which of these novel isoforms should be interrogated and to predict their functionality remain elusive. To address this, we developed a computational framework, Centroid-based Isoform Pathway Inference (CIPI), which contextualizes novel genes and isoforms relative to reference genes with similar cell-type expression patterns. Rather than relying solely on host-gene annotation or similarity to known protein domains, CIPI constructs expression-based neighborhoods that, combined with pathway analyses such as GO, KEGG, or Reactome, enable inference of pathway-level contextualization of individual isoforms according to their biologically meaningful neighbors. Combining CIPI with pathway analyses provides a biological context to novel isoforms, enabling a hypothesis-generating approach for prioritizing novel isoforms across the isonome.

last_author.name: Ebbert, M. T. W.
last_author.affiliation: University of Kentucky

preprints.title: Biological and technical spatial variation in spatial transcriptomics
preprints.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics technologies enable the identification of spatially variable genes that can shed light on tissue structure and function. However, spatial variability of gene expression can be due not only to biological function but also technical artifact. We develop a model for spatially variable capture that forms part of a bursty transcription model, allowing us to distinguish biological variability from spatially variable technical noise. Our approach is implemented in a program called stipple, which we demonstrate can be useful for identifying and interpreting spatial gene expression variation from spatial transcriptomics assays.

last_author.name: Pachter, L.
last_author.affiliation: California Institute of Technology

preprints.title: CHORUS: A proteome-scale atlas of membrane interaction interfaces constructed using cross-protein language model embeddings from sequences alone
preprints.abstract: Membrane proteins drive vital cellular signaling and bioenergetics yet resolving their physical interaction interfaces remains hindered by the paucity of experimental complexes and the breakdown of sequence alignments across hydrophobic bilayers. Here, we present CHORUS, a sequence-only deep-learning framework that decodes interaction sites across membrane proteins without requiring 3D structures, multiple sequence alignments (MSAs), or predefined partner identities. By systematically synthesizing complementary latent representations across diverse protein language model (pLM) families and functional layer depths, CHORUS outperforms 18 established sequence- and structure-based methods across 4,655 homology-isolated test contexts (average precision: 0.643), demonstrating amplified predictive capacity within the lipid-embedded core (0.746). We show that CHORUS delineates quaternary contact boundaries across megadalton respiratory supercomplexes directly from sequences alone (0.984). We deliver the CHORUS Atlas (https://chorus.atlas.sunnylab.org), providing precomputed, residue-resolved interaction landscapes for 80,619 reviewed transmembrane proteins spanning 4,918 species and 33.7 million residues to empower interactome-scale discovery and allosteric therapeutic design.

last_author.name: Sun, J.
last_author.affiliation: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

preprints.corresponding_institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

preprints.title: CLARA: Compound Library Active Learning with Reasoning Agents
preprints.abstract: Batch active learning for ligand discovery requires a recurring decision about whether to exploit high predicted affinity, reduce model uncertainty, or broaden chemical coverage. We test whether a language model can make this strategy-level decision while candidate ranking and label revelation remain controlled by a deterministic Gaussian-process environment. Across four protein targets, ten paired seeds, and a 360-compound assay budget, a GPT-5.6 Sol agent outperformed random sampling in all 40 matched campaigns. Its final top-2\% recall was 0.412 on D2R, 0.374 on Mpro, 0.448 on TYK2, and 0.683 on USP7. It was statistically tied with the strongest fixed policy on Mpro and USP7 but underperformed target-specific leaders on D2R and TYK2. The agent shifted from exploration-oriented early batches toward exploitation and produced 686 testable threshold claims with an 86.3\% atomic success rate, although 19.8\% of forecasts were not numerically scorable. In 200 prespecified information-ablation campaigns, removing uncertainty, diversity, or memory caused only small endpoint changes, while shuffling explanatory evidence reproduced the full allocation path in 39 of 40 paired campaigns. A deterministic 80\% availability constraint reduced recall on every target but preserved the target-dependent pattern of wins and losses. These results support language-model strategy control as a feasible and auditable layer.

last_author.name: Singh, R. K.
last_author.affiliation: Shiv Nadar University

preprints.title: Cancer cachexia overrides sex-specific traits in Drosophila
preprints.abstract: Cancer cachexia, a metabolic syndrome characterized by pathologic weight loss, dramatically limits therapeutic options and reduces survival. While the mechanisms by which tumors induce wasting of distant organs (particularly muscle and adipose tissues) remain incompletely understood, the influence of biological sex on cachexia progression is even less clear. Here we investigated phenotypic and molecular manifestations of cachexia in both sexes using a model of inducible intestinal tumors in Drosophila. We show that tumor progression leads to the development of severe cachexia both in males and in females manifested by organ atrophies and an inflammatory state. Nevertheless, both phenotypical and molecular cachexic alterations exhibit striking differences between sexes. Transcriptomic analysis show that many genes differentially expressed at high levels in males under normal conditions become downregulated during cachexia, while their expression is upregulated in cachexic females, and reciprocally. Together, sex-specific deregulation in gene expression and metabolic profiles ultimately converge towards a molecular cachexic state that erase or diminish many sex-specific differences otherwise characteristic of healthy males and females. These findings highlight the interplay between oncogenic stress and biological sex in shaping cachexia phenotypes, shedding light on how sex influences the development of cancer cachexia.

last_author.name: Polesello, C.
last_author.affiliation: CNRS Délégation Midi-Pyrénées

preprints.title: Capture-(Hi)C analysis with PostChicago: Integrative metaprofiling and quantitative comparison of chromatin interactions
preprints.abstract: Functionally linking enhancers to gene promoters at high resolution often entails analysis of 3C datasets, including viewpoint-based methods such as Capture-(Hi)C. Quantitative comparison across samples and experiments, together with visualization and integration of promoter interactions with other datasets are of critical importance. While existing statistical tools identify significant interactions and quantify underlying signal, systematically comparing the shape and extent of this signal across large sets of intervals remains challenging. Moreover, experimental artefacts, such as inefficient crosslinking, can affect downstream interpretation, but are difficult to detect systematically. Here we introduce PostChicago, an R/Bioconductor package that fills this gap. Building upon the widely used interaction-calling package Chicago, PostChicago provides a complete workflow for quality control, visualization, integration and quantitative analysis of promoter interactions between multiple samples, including annotation and quantification of genomic regions based on external datasets. PostChicago extends visual quantitative comparisons beyond individual viewpoints by computing normalized metaprofiles around large sets of intervals that visualize the distribution of interaction signal, enabling comparison between narrow and broad interaction patterns. We further demonstrate how PostChicago can identify experimental crosslinking artefacts. Together, PostChicago enables integrative, shape-sensitive analysis and quality control of promoter Capture-(Hi)C datasets at a scale that would otherwise require extensive custom scripting.

last_author.name: Feldmann, A.
last_author.affiliation: German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ)

preprints.title: Centromeric islands constrain CENP-A domain size and position
preprints.abstract: Centromere identity is specified epigenetically by nucleosomes containing the histone H3 variant CENP-A, yet centromeres are almost invariably embedded within repetitive DNA, suggesting that underlying DNA sequences contribute to the organization of centromeric chromatin. In Drosophila melanogaster, CENP-A primarily occupies retroelement-rich islands flanked by simple satellite DNA, but their functional contribution remains unclear. Here, we delete the ~50-kb island Giglio from centromere 3 while preserving the flanking satellites and residual CENP-A chromatin. Despite removal of the DNA sequence associated with most centromeric CENP-A, centromere identity and overall CENP-A levels are preserved at the native locus, indicating that the island itself is not required for centromere identity. Instead, Giglio deletion increases variability in CENP-A chromatin organization, producing highly heterogeneous domain sizes and preferential redistribution of the CENP-A domain into the adjacent dodeca satellite. Together, these findings demonstrate that Giglio is dispensable for centromere identity but constrains the size and position of the CENP-A domain, establishing centromeric islands as key determinants of CENP-A domain architecture.

last_author.name: Mellone, B. G.
last_author.affiliation: University of Connecticut

preprints.title: Characterisation of Genetically-Derived Patient Clusters Highlights Genetic Heterogeneity of Inflammatory Bowel Disease
preprints.abstract: Background and aims. Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is a complex immune-mediated condition with a strong genetic contribution. The genetics of IBD are highly complex, with inflammation, autoimmunity, and mucosal immunity pathways involved in its pathogenicity. GenePy is a gene-level disease burden metric. The integration of clinical and genetic data and the application of machine learning methods can aid patient stratification for personalised care. Methods. Lists of consensus IBD pathway genes were curated. GenePy scores were computed from whole exome sequencing data. A K-Means algorithm was optimised using clustering quality and stability metrics on the GenePy scores of genes in each IBD pathway, and the results replicated in three independent IBD cohorts (SPARC IBD, MSCCR IBD, and Southampton IBD). Chi-square tests assessed the association between cluster assignment and phenotypic features, and were multiple test corrected via Benjamini-Hochberg FDR. Results. A strong association was replicated for NOD signalling genes driving IBD subtype, Crohns disease behaviour, and IBD surgery across all cohorts, as well as granuloma in Southampton IBD. This was mainly driven by NOD2. Similar genetic clustering patterns were observed across all cohorts, with additional phenotypic enrichment in clusters driven by NLRP1 (surgery in MSCCR IBD), and nominally significant enrichment for disease behaviour linked to BIRC2 (B2 in Southampton IBD and B2B3 in SPARC IBD). Conclusions. This analysis identified a common genetic architecture across NOD signalling genes across IBD cohorts, replicated a signal for NOD2 as a monogenic driver of disease with a strong phenotypic enrichment, and identified other putative genetic drivers of IBD, such as the NLRP1 gene.

last_author.name: Ashton, J. J.
last_author.affiliation: Human Genetics and Genomic Medicine, University of Southampton, Southampton, UK

preprints.corresponding_institution: Human Genetics and Genomic Medicine, University of Southampton, Southampton, UK

preprints.title: Common cis-eQTLs do not explain chromosome 21 expression deviations from the ploidy expectation in Down syndrome
preprints.abstract: Down syndrome (DS) results from trisomy 21 (T21), the triplication of human chromosome 21 (HSA21). On average, genes on HSA21 are overexpressed at the expected 1.5-fold increase. A small subset of HSA21 genes is expressed closer to euploid levels. Could local genetic regulatory variation explain deviations from the expected dosage? Using the largest DS-specific transcriptomic dataset to date from the Human Trisome Project (HTP) and GTEx expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs), we tested whether local genetic regulatory variation contributes to gene-specific buffering or amplification of HSA21 dosage effects in DS. We compared the bulk RNA-seq profiles of protein-coding genes, lncRNAs, and pseudogenes from whole-blood samples of 274 participants with T21 and 80 euploid (D21) participants. We filtered out genes with low read counts or high genomic repeat content and applied ploidy correction to the differential expression analysis. We found 13 genes that differed significantly from the expected fold change. We cross-referenced GTEx whole-blood eQTLs (cis window 1 {+/-} Mb) with the 13 deviating genes. A common cis-eQTL was detected for 8 of the 10 testable genes. However, 59 of 99 HSA21 genes that had the expected fold change had significant cis-eQTLs. Additionally, T21 participants carry the eQTL alleles at similar frequencies to GTEx donors. Therefore, cis-eQTLs explain differences between people with T21, not the difference between T21 and D21. Overall, common cis-regulatory variation acts on HSA21 genes in T21 as it does in euploid blood, but it does not explain which genes deviate from the ploidy expectation.

preprints.title: Constructed Negatives Shape the Evaluation of Sequence-Based Protein--Protein Interaction Models
preprints.abstract: Many machine-learning tasks, including representation learning, rely on negative examples that are constructed rather than directly observed. This issue is especially important for protein--protein interaction (PPI) prediction, where experimentally established non-interactions are scarce. PPI models are therefore commonly trained and evaluated against sampled, unobserved protein pairs treated as negatives. We study how this construction affects model comparison. Keeping positives, protein-disjoint splits, class balance, and model selection fixed, we vary training and evaluation negatives independently across six constructions and four sequence-based models, three of which use protein language model (pLM) representations. Changing only the test negatives shifts AUPRC by up to 0.26, and the top-ranked architecture changes with the construction. Negatives matched to true partners in pLM representation space reduce all pLM-based models to near-chance performance, and shuffling partners within each class shows that the original pairing contributes little to AUROC. Constructed training negatives rarely outperform uniform sampling: on external data, they underperform it in 108 of 120 comparisons for the pLM-based models, with gains never exceeding 0.05 AUROC and losses up to 0.23. We release splits, negative-generation procedures, and evaluation code that allow training and evaluation negatives to be varied separately. Our results show that with constructed negatives, model comparisons are not just noisy but systematically sensitive to how negatives are defined, a methodological choice that is often left implicit.

last_author.name: Laine, E.
last_author.affiliation: Sorbonne Universite, CNRS, IBPS,  Laboratoire de Biologie Computationnelle et Quantitative (LCQB)

preprints.corresponding_institution: Sorbonne Universite, CNRS, IBPS,  Laboratoire de Biologie Computationnelle et Quantitative (LCQB)

preprints.title: Cross-species analysis identifies APOBEC3-associated spliceosomal snRNA hypermutability
preprints.abstract: Spliceosomal small nuclear RNA (snRNA) genes show unusually high germline mutation rates, with R-loop formation previously implicated in this mutability. Our cross-species rare-variant and de novo mutation analyses show that hypermutability is concentrated in RNA polymerase II-transcribed spliceosomal snRNA genes, with strong enrichment in primates but a much weaker excess in rodents and chicken, consistent with lineage differences in APOBEC3 repertoires. Human Pol II-transcribed spliceosomal snRNA genes show mutational strand asymmetry, APOBEC3-associated mutational signatures and strong APOBEC3B binding signals. R-loops are also frequent at these loci, including in mouse genes with much weaker hypermutability, indicating that R-loop formation alone is insufficient to explain the phenotype. Together, cross-species comparisons support lineage-specific APOBEC3 activity, rather than R-loop formation alone, as a major contributor to spliceosomal snRNA gene hypermutability.

last_author.name: Li, C.
last_author.affiliation: Sun Yat-sen University

preprints.title: Decomposing scanner batch effects and their impact on pathology foundation models
preprints.abstract: Pathology foundation models (PFMs) are expected to represent the same tissue in the same way on any scanner, but their embeddings still carry scanner signals. Scanner-related image differences and the scanner sensitivity of PFMs have each been described. How tissue-dependent changes in color and spatial frequency relate to shifts in PFM representations, and what this means for correction, is less understood. We imaged 103 slides from 37 normal tissue types on six scanners (PanNormal; 95,780 matched locations) and used the real paired images as targets. We used the public PLISM dataset for external validation. First, we decomposed scanner differences into image properties. Color and spatial frequency changed together, by amounts that depended on tissue type. Second, corrections that matched these measured properties brought images closer to the target more reliably than representations. Pix2Pix reduced the image residual by 69% but increased UNI distance to the target by 27%. The same frequency matching helped one scanner and hurt another. Probes still distinguished corrected from real target embeddings after every correction. Third, changing one frequency band at a time showed that PFMs differ in how strongly each band moves them and whether it moves them toward the target. Across eight PFMs pretrained on whole-slide image tiles, the models that moved least under these small changes were the most robust to real scanner differences (Spearman {rho}=-0.90). Aligning images and aligning representations are therefore different goals. The gap between them depends on scanner, tissue, and model.

preprints.title: Do LLM Proposers Improve Budgeted Search for Ionizable Lipids?
preprints.abstract: Efficient lipid design under limited experimental budgets is a central challenge in computational chemistry and drug discovery. We introduce LEAF (Lipid Evolutionary Adaptive Framework), a matched-budget protocol for testing whether language-model proposers improve combinatorial molecular search relative to classical baselines. The study uses a 30,044-candidate ionizable-lipid space, a frozen Gaussian-process oracle fitted to experimental potency labels, and a separate active-learning surrogate. Four language models evaluated over eight seeds and three splits show no significant improvement over genetic-algorithm or random-search baselines. For Llama 8B, 79.1% of acquisition-selected queries repeat previously evaluated archive members. Removing duplicates reduces the performance gap on some splits but increases proposal cost and can prevent budget exhaustion. Larger models reduce duplication without establishing superiority or equivalence. Exploratory scored prompts and stricter novelty controls yield positive median differences against the genetic algorithm, yet wide intervals and shared-seed dependence preclude stronger conclusions. A validated single-assay reanalysis preserves the chemotype-cold deficit at a smaller numerical scale, and exploratory expected hypervolume improvement does not reverse the result. Follow-up checks address whether proposers genuinely use injected evidence. These checks include a zero-shot leakage probe, rank-only and chain-of-thought-rationale prompts, a score-shuffle perturbation, an evidence-conflict probe, and a genuine reasoning-mode proposer. They show measurable engagement with supplied information without a corresponding performance gain. LEAF isolates proposal quality as the experimental variable and documents a concrete failure mode of zero-shot LLM proposers under controlled budgets.

preprints.title: Dual-graph deconvolution of enzyme fitness: an interpretable framework to identify and explain catalytic modulators
preprints.abstract: Models trained on protein sequences can predict mutational effects, but their outputs represent a convolution of different phenotypes. Isolating stability-independent activity effects is essential for rational enzyme design, allosteric drug design and functional annotation, yet existing pLM-based deconvolution methods lack interpretability. Here, we introduce a hybrid framework that pairs stability predictors with probabilistic graphical models of coevolution. Benchmarked on all enzymes with available multidimensional deep mutational scanning data, our framework isolates stability-independent activity effects with a fidelity that matches analogous pLM-based approaches. Crucially, we reveal biophysically plausible communication pathways that align with previous knowledge and that we validate with experimental data across a diverse set of targets. This hybrid approach merges statistical and geometric deep learning into a zero-shot, explainable tool for targeted engineering and mechanistic discovery.

last_author.name: Marks, D. S.
last_author.affiliation: Harvard Medical School

preprints.title: Efficient approximate Bayesian inference for large, heterogeneous biological datasets
preprints.abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) offers a route to connect biological data with mechanistic models. At the frontier of biology, datasets continue to grow in scale and richness, and increasingly record heterogeneity between individual observations that a mechanistic model can take into account. Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) remains a popular approach to SBI due to its ease of use, but incorporating this heterogeneity often requires a separate simulation of each observation, which is prohibitively expensive at scale. A previously proposed technique, minibatch Sequential Monte Carlo ABC (SMC ABC), reduces this cost by simulating a fixed-size random subset of observations for each proposal, at the price of sampling noise that limits precision. Here, we present an adaptive minibatch approach that uses small batches during early exploration and increases the batch size as the posterior is refined. The adaptive batch size is set by the target precision and does not grow with the size of the dataset, so the savings over full-data SMC ABC increase for larger datasets. We demonstrate the method on synthetic biological models and on real single-cell gene-expression data that vary in scale and type of heterogeneity, including cell geometry and initial condition. In each case, the adaptive scheme obtains posteriors close to those of full-data SMC ABC at a fraction of the cost. Altogether, adaptive minibatching improves the tradeoff between speed and precision in SMC ABC and opens the door to mechanistic inference on large, heterogeneous biological datasets.

preprints.title: Epithelial Self-Organization Patterns the Tadpole Oral Disc
preprints.abstract: Vertebrate epidermal organs are generally patterned through epithelial-mesenchymal interactions, but whether such interactions are essential for all epidermal organs remains unclear. Here we show that the elaborate oral disc of anuran tadpoles arises by partitioning a continuous oral epithelium into developmentally distinct jaw, tooth-row and papilla modules, in the absence of a mesenchymal organizer. Spatially restricted epithelial programs specify, maintain and differentiate these modules, enabling their semi-independent development. Perturbation of lef1, hoxc13, sox7 and pitx2 selectively disrupts individual modules. The resulting module-specific reductions, expansions and rearrangements mirror oral-disc configurations that have evolves repeatedly across anurans. These findings indicate that differential deployment of shared epithelial programs can generates selectable variation in the tadpole oral disc, allowing transient larval feeding structures to diversify independently of adult ecology and enabling tadpoles to exploit diverse ecological niches. Epidermal self-organization can therefore generate structural complexity, promote functional diversification and enhance evolvability in transient vertebrate organs.

last_author.name: Wang, S.

preprints.title: Filling the Missing Puzzle: Integrating Interaction and Evolutionary Information to Enhance Protein Fitness Prediction in Inverse Folding
preprints.abstract: Protein inverse folding, which infers compatible amino acid sequences from a given backbone structure, is central to rational protein design. Current methods rely largely on sequence recovery rate as the evaluation metric, emphasizing structural compatibility but seldom addressing function. Yet functional activity depends on the proper network of non-covalent interactions-protein-ligand contacts being a prime example. We argue that function-oriented protein design is governed by three complementary constraints: structural, interaction, and evolutionary, none of which are handled in a unified manner by existing pretrained models. To bridge this gap, we introduce zPolaron, a graph neural network built on protein-ligand complexes for functional protein design. zPolaron represents residues and ligand atoms as a heterogeneous graph and jointly encodes structural, interaction, and evolutionary information by fusing physical-interaction-enhanced graph representations with ESM-2 embeddings. Across multiple fitness prediction benchmarks, zPolaron outperforms all baselines, with gains evident across structural, interaction, and evolutionary dimensions. Wet-lab experiments further confirm its utility in functional enzyme screening and design: the optimized CalA6-D205A-S160G mutant achieves a 17.84-fold improvement in activity, while the CalB-I121M mutant yields a 1.91-fold increase. Together, these results show that integrating interaction and evolutionary information fills the missing puzzle of inverse folding, enhancing protein fitness prediction beyond structural compatibility. zPolaron is available at https://github.com/zelixirSH/zPolaron.

last_author.name: Li, W.

preprints.title: Forecasting next-year change in antimicrobial resistance genes in Klebsiella pneumoniae and Acinetobacter baumannii from genomic surveillance data
preprints.abstract: Background: Surveillance tells laboratories which antimicrobial resistance genes are circulating now, but not which will change next. We built a model that forecasts, for each resistance gene and year, whether the following year brings a previously unseen allele (sequence variant), called emergence, or a change in the most common allele, called turnover. We tested it separately in Klebsiella pneumoniae and Acinetobacter baumannii. Results: We used genomes annotated with AMRFinderPlus: 2,385 gene-years across 331 genes for K.pneumoniae and 1,059 across 216 for A. baumannii. To remove the effect of sequencing effort, each gene-year was sampled to 10 records and the analysis repeated 25 times. Models were trained on earlier years and tested on later ones, and on genes held out of training. On later years every model ranked genes by risk better than simple baselines in both organisms, and results for held-out genes were close. In K.pneumoniae, turnover was predicted better than emergence (best area under the ROC curve, AUROC, 0.909 versus 0.819). In A. baumannii the order reversed (emergence 0.789, turnover 0.722). The two events also relied on different features. Emergence depended mainly on how many alleles a gene had already accumulated, in both organisms. Turnover in K. pneumoniae depended mainly on how dominant the leading allele already was, and a stability index added a small gain. In A. baumannii it was spread across many weaker features. There, 56% of changes in the leading allele involved only alleles already seen, against 23% in K. pneumoniae, which may make them harder to predict. Conclusions: Changes in resistance genes can be forecast a year ahead from routine genomic surveillance data, including for genes the model has not seen. How well it works, and what it depends on, differs between organisms, so models should be built and validated for each organism, not assumed to transfer. Such models could help laboratories decide which resistance genes to monitor most closely. Keywords: antimicrobial resistance; genomic surveillance; forecasting; machine learning; allele dynamics; Klebsiella pneumoniae; Acinetobacter baumannii

preprints.title: GLARE: Genomic Language model for Automated Repetitive Element classification
preprints.abstract: Reliable classification of transposable elements (TEs) is important for genome annotation and evolutionary analysis, yet remains challenging: TE families differ widely across taxa, reference databases label them inconsistently, and many TEs are represented only by degraded copies. We introduce GLARE (Genomic Language model for Automated Repetitive Element classification), a TE classifier built by fine-tuning a genomic language model on harmonized PanTEon and Repbase reference data to predict TE superfamily across 32 superfamilies in 11 orders. Among the genomic language models compared, Nucleotide Transformer v3 provided the strongest representation. Built on this backbone, GLARE exceeded all nine classifiers in the PanTEon benchmark, reaching 0.966 weighted superfamily F1 on its 30-superfamily task. GLARE also showed stronger generalization to clades absent from training, consistently exceeding state-of-the-art classifiers on holdouts spanning three taxonomic ranks: the order Poales, the phylum Arthropoda, and the kingdom Fungi. Training on both PanTEon and Repbase reduced the performance drop seen when a single-source model was applied to the other database. Under simulated sequence decay, GLARE was the most robust classifier tested, and it performed best on independently curated degraded libraries. These findings show that genomic language models fine-tuned on harmonized multi-source references can classify TEs robustly under the taxonomic, database, and sequence-quality shifts that matter in practice. GLARE is available at https://code.jgi.doe.gov/NHaas/glare.

preprints.title: GenDiMug: a generic inclusive multigraph framework to analyze genomic organizations and -omics data at multiple scales
preprints.abstract: After decades of investigation, analyses of genome organization remain challenging. This is because genome descriptions are very information-rich and usually rendered as a linear map of genomic features corresponding to an ordered list of position intervals on a nucleic acid macromolecular backbone. This formalism, while accurate, is not fully optimized to mathematically analyze all genome structural properties, in particular the relations between genomic features, nor to integrate large amounts of -omics data, such as transcriptomes, epigenomes, proteomes, meltomes or chromatin accessibility data, which are increasingly available. We therefore developed GenDiMug, a tool that uses a network representation of the genome as a backbone, providing a natural framework to integrate spatial and ontogenetic relationships between genomic features and multi-omics data. We illustrate how this generic approach can be applied to all sorts of genomes, both to visualize genomic topology at contig and chromosomal scales at base-pair resolution, and to analyze genome positional effects using various graph metrics. Using GenDiMug, we further reveal clumping of genes with similar expression levels in eukaryotic genomes and their possible circadian regulation in a photosynthetic alga.
